[BURSEVI:v6p59#3/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The disbelievers had the worst traits: disbelief in the Creator and resurrection, immersion in worldly love, and oppression; their destruction came because of their injustice.
[BURSEVI:v6p59#3/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Ghuthaʾ is what a flood carries along its surface: foam, leaves, and sticks; the idiom 'the valley swept him away' means that someone perished.

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p33#4/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | On the view that the people were Thamud, Gabriel's cry destroyed them; if they were ʿAd, this conflicts with reports that a violent wind destroyed them.

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p33#4/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Alternatively, الصيحة means a terrible punishment or overwhelming torment, as in the poetic idiom that time cried out against the Barmakids.

[ALUSI-FULL:v18p33#4/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | بعدا can report their distance or function as a curse; distance is opposite nearness, while the second verbal form is used for destruction, and the noun means distance from mercy, good, salvation, or utter ruin.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r11] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The wrongdoers are the unbelievers: they wronged themselves by associating partners with God and wronged Hud by accusing him of lying about God. | mentions 31:13, 23:38

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Taking them is a metaphor for destroying them.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Attributing destruction to the cry is a rational metaphor: the cry is the cause of destruction or accompanies its cause, the air tearing when the thunderbolt falls.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The bāʾ marks accompaniment: the destruction was just, not an assault, because their wrongdoing made them deserve it.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | غثاء is what a flood carries, such as dry sticks and leaves.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v18p58/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | This is a concise state simile: like flood debris, they decayed and piled in one place, dying all together.
